packs.title: Waterline Wonder
packs.promise: Find Amsterdam in the frames, folds and reflections beside the water.

q.s: Collect depth one bridge shape at a time.
st: Choose a comfortable public-pavement viewpoint at Reguliersgracht and Herengracht, keeping away from the unguarded water edge and cycle traffic.
Look along the canal for a near arch, a farther arch or railing, and a reflection. You do not need to see or count every bridge.
Describe one detail that becomes smaller with distance and one detail the water changes.
Save your three finds and the two comparisons.

q.s: Collect a small exhibition from the building’s outside.
st: Find a comfortable public view of the Rijksmuseum from the Museumplein side. No admission ticket or entrance queue is needed.
Find three exterior contrasts: red brick against pale stone, a pointed roof against sky, and a deep opening against a flat wall.
Give each contrast a short label in your own words, as if you were arranging three observations in a tiny exhibition.
Save your three labels and choose an opening piece.

q.t: Fold a Building in Your Mind
q.s: Turn an architectural curve into an imaginary paper shape.
st: From the public side of Prins Hendrikkade, choose a comfortable view of Arcam, Amsterdam’s architecture centre. Exhibition entry is optional and outside the mission.
Notice how the metal surface folds and curves around the compact building, then find an edge where metal meets glass.
Imagine one sheet of paper becoming that shape. Describe two folds and one curve in a short note or simple sketch; no actual paper construction is necessary.
Give your imagined shape a title and save it.

packs.title: Brick and Water
packs.promise: Explore western Amsterdam through park forms, expressive brickwork and harbour views.

q.s: Make a tiny storyboard from a cinema frontage.
st: Look at the cinema frontage from an open public position, or use the tourism authority’s photograph. Choose a doorway, a window and a roof detail.
Draw three small frames using those forms: an arrival, a closer look and a departure. Use your own imagined sequence rather than copying a film or poster.
Add one sentence describing a change between frames. Simple shapes or a written three-part sequence are enough.

q.s: Turn a housing block’s curved forms into a small design.
st: Use public pavement to look at the red-brick housing block, or use the linked building photograph. Keep a respectful distance from homes and entrances.
Find a curved brick form and a straight window edge. Make a small design that combines one curve with one straight line.
Make a second version by changing the curve. Save both and describe how the change affects the balance; museum entry and detailed drawing skills are unnecessary.

q.s: Find a repeating pattern in a long public seat.
st: Follow an open part of the park’s public path and find a long wave-shaped bench, or use the installed photograph shared by its engineer.
Find a repeated strip, a change in curve and a gap. Describe how the yellow and blue parts overlap in your chosen view.
Save those three details as a sketch or note. Add a small comparison between the bench’s curve and the path beside it.
